meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Hold fast to dreams, for if dreams die, life is a broken-winged bird that cannot fly'?
meta.ogDescription: Real Langston Hughes: the first stanza of his poem “Dreams” (The World Tomorrow, 1923). The words are authentic; the viral one-liner just drops the line breaks.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: This is the genuine opening stanza of Hughes’s short poem “Dreams,” first published in the magazine The World Tomorrow in May 1923. The words are authentic; the popular one-line form simply runs the four short verses together and drops the address “my son” that stood in the original 1923 printing (Hughes later revised it out).

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: The Dream Keeper and Other Poems (1932); The Collected Poems of Langston Hughes (Knopf, 1994)

source.excerpt:
Hold fast to dreams, my son,
For if dreams die
Life is a broken-winged bird
That cannot fly.

Hold fast to dreams, O boy,
For when dreams go
Life is a barren field
Frozen with snow.
trail: The Lehigh digital anthology ↗ dates first publication to The World Tomorrow, May 1923, and prints the original stanzas verbatim.
The Academy of American Poets ↗ hosts the standard modern text — “Hold fast to dreams / For if dreams die / Life is a broken-winged bird / That cannot fly” — matching the quoted words exactly.
Because the poem was first published in 1923, its original text is in the U.S. public domain, though modern collected editions carry an estate copyright notice.
source.excerptNote: The original 1923 printing addressed “my son” and “O boy”; Hughes later removed those, and the version circulated today (and shown on poets.org ↗) simply reads “Hold fast to dreams / For if dreams die…” The viral one-line quote flattens the four verses into a single sentence.

author.name: Langston Hughes
author.heading: About Langston Hughes
author.metaLine: 1901–1967 · American poet, novelist & leading voice of the Harlem Renaissance
author.bio: Langston Hughes (1901–1967) was one of the defining writers of the Harlem Renaissance, celebrated for poems that fused everyday Black American speech with the rhythms of jazz and blues. “Dreams” is one of his earliest and most anthologized short poems, written in his early twenties. Its plainspoken metaphors have kept it in classrooms and graduation speeches for a century.

misattribution.heading: Correctly credited — but usually misquoted in form
misattribution.intro: This one is a rarity among viral quotes: the attribution to Langston Hughes is correct. What travels online is a lightly garbled form of a real poem, not a fabrication.

items.why: The words are authentic, but the internet renders the four short verses as one run-on prose sentence — “Hold fast to dreams, for if dreams die, life is a broken-winged bird that cannot fly” — erasing the line breaks that give the poem ↗ its shape.
The first 1923 printing ↗ read “Hold fast to dreams, my son” and “Hold fast to dreams, O boy”; Hughes later cut those addresses, so most quotations (rightly) omit them.
This is the poem “Dreams,” sometimes muddled with Hughes’s separate poem “The Dream Keeper” (from The Weary Blues, 1926) — a different text entirely.

misattribution.truthLine: Verdict: really Langston Hughes. It’s the opening stanza of his poem “Dreams” ↗, first published in 1923 — the only liberty taken is flattening its verse into a single line.

context.heading: Why it endures
lead: Written when Hughes was barely into his twenties, “Dreams” distills a whole ethic into eight lines: hold onto aspiration, because a life without it is crippled and cold. Its two images — a bird that can no longer fly, a field frozen barren — are simple enough for a child yet stark enough to stay with adults, which is why the poem migrated from the page onto posters, murals, and countless commencement stages.

The line’s ubiquity is also why it gets flattened. Stripped of its verse form and typed into a single sentence for a graphic or a caption, it reads like a maxim rather than a poem — but unlike most “maxims” pinned to famous names, this one is genuinely, verifiably theirs.
